<p class="section__label">News · Doctoral thesis · from the TAMARYS network</p>

<h1 class="thesis-h1">Thermal emission below the wavelength, from far field to near field</h1>

<p class="thesis-lead">On <strong>29 June 2026</strong>, <strong>Kyriaki Kontou</strong> defended her
doctoral thesis, <em>“Far- and near-field thermal infrared emission of planar samples including
micrometric areas,”</em> at the Center for Energy and Thermal Sciences of Lyon (CETHIL), INSA Lyon.
The work asks what happens to thermal emission when the emitting area becomes comparable to, or
smaller than, the thermal wavelength, a regime where Planck’s law and geometrical optics no longer
tell the whole story.</p>

<h2 class="thesis-h2">Abstract</h2>

<p><em>In the author’s words:</em></p>

<p>This thesis investigates the thermal emission through single apertures with radii comparable to
or smaller than the thermal wavelength, combining theoretical modeling with far-field experiments.
Kirchhoff and Bethe scattering models, adapted to our system with a metallic screen attached to a
substrate, predict deviations from Planck’s law and an emissivity enhancement for polar dielectrics,
where evanescent waves are scattered to the far field. In the far field, FTIR microscopy in
reflection mode allows to characterize these single apertures and reveals experimentally deviations
from geometrical optics. A detailed investigation of the direct emission measurements using
different modulation methods on FTIR microscopy shows also the challenges regarding single object
detection and parasitic signals. Finally, in the near field, an inverse method based on scanning
thermal microscopy (SThM) is proposed to retrieve spectral information from heat-flux measurements,
opening a path toward the development of novel spectral characterization methods without the need
of a spectroscope.</p>

<h2 class="thesis-h2">Why it matters for emissivity</h2>

<p>Emissivity is usually treated as a property of a surface large enough for geometrical optics to
hold. Kontou’s work tests that assumption at its limit: when the aperture shrinks to the scale of the
thermal wavelength, evanescent surface waves of polar dielectrics can be scattered into the far field
and raise the apparent emissivity, while measuring such a small object brings its own artefacts. The
far-field FTIR-microscopy methods and the first steps towards a near-field inverse method using
scanning microscopy methods developed here are directly relevant to anyone characterising
micro-structured emitters, patterned surfaces or small samples.</p>

<p>The defence was announced to the <a href="/network/networks/tamarys.html">GDR TAMARYS</a> research
network; reported here with the author’s agreement and that of the network’s coordination, after
<a href="/events-news/news/perrin-terrin-thesis-2026.html">Jean-Baptiste Perrin-Terrin’s thesis</a> in
June.</p>

<p class="thesis-coda">Our warmest congratulations to Dr Kontou and her supervisors.</p>
